answer:
**Answer: SES (socioeconomic status).** The effect of SES on BA degree completion decreases from ≈+0.36 to ≈−0.23 and loses significance when race and academic characteristics (ASVAB ability composite, class percentile) are added to the model.

**Natural-language hypothesis for submission:** "The apparent positive effect of socioeconomic status (SES) on BA degree completion is not a direct causal effect but is mediated by academic resources and racial composition. In a baseline logistic model, SES carries a significant positive coefficient of ≈0.36 (log-odds); when race dummies and academic characteristics — the ASVAB composite ability score and percentile in class — are added, the SES coefficient flips sign to ≈−0.23 and becomes statistically insignificant. This is because SES is strongly correlated with academic performance (r ≈ 0.46 with the ASVAB composite, 0.30 with class percentile, which itself correlates 0.70 with ability) and with race (Whites have higher SES, ability, and class rank, and much higher BA rates: 3.5% vs ~1.4% for Black/Hispanic respondents). Once academic performance and race are held constant, family socioeconomic background adds no independent positive contribution to finishing a BA — academic achievement channels (and can even slightly reverse) the SES advantage."

**Best-matching specification (full model):** logit(BA) ~ SES + race dummies (ref = White) + ABILITY + PERCENTILE → SES = −0.2316 (HC1 SE 0.1113) vs ground-truth −0.2293 (|Δ| = 0.0023); adding sex gives −0.2379. Baseline candidates: SES alone = 0.4729; SES + sex + race = 0.3548 (closest to 0.3636). No other variable shows this signature (family size is always strongly negative, −0.52 to −0.63; sex ≈ +0.25; race dummies ±0.2–0.5), so SES is uniquely identified.

payload.hypothesis: The apparent positive effect of socioeconomic status (SES) on BA degree completion is mediated by academic resources and racial composition: in a baseline model SES has a significant positive log-odds coefficient (~0.36), but when race and academic characteristics (ASVAB composite ability score, percentile in class) are added, the SES coefficient flips to ~-0.23 and becomes insignificant. SES is strongly correlated with ability (r~0.46) and class rank (r~0.30), and race stratifies both SES and academic performance, so academic achievement channels the SES-BA association; family SES adds no independent positive effect on BA completion.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 rows, no missing values); inspected distributions, missingness, outcome coding (BA boolean, 236 positives); ran nested logistic regressions with HC1 robust SEs: SES-only baseline (+0.47, p~1e-9), +sex/family size (+0.84), +race (+0.82), +academics; exhaustive specification search showed only SES reproduces the ~+0.36 -> ~-0.23 sign-flip signature; best-matching full model (SES + race + ASVAB composite + class percentile, without family size) gives SES = -0.2316 (target -0.2293); verified PERCENTILE IN CLASS sign convention (higher = better rank, corr +0.17 with BA); influence diagnostics (dfbeta trimming) confirm the negative near-zero effect is not outlier-driven; probit and classical-SE variants push the full-model SES p-value above 0.05, consistent with 'becoming insignificant'.
